157:### 4.3 Endpoints
212:  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
248:2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
254:3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.
417:handshake timeout and the subscriber overflow behave as §4.1 says under
425:memory at a time (§4.1 is read with that change), and the Bonjour
435:**A1 — Identity and an authenticated read-only host.** `identity.json` (id, certificate, `server_name` and the listen preference: off the LAN by default, loopback until enabled), the key in the Keychain under its installation's account, `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`. `ports::remote`, `adapters/remote.rs` with the bounds of §4.1 and the two-step content handoff, a fake, the `Effect` and `AppAction` arms, the allowlist, the redaction function. The pairing window and QR code in the settings menu, the paired-devices dialog with scope and Revoke, `devices.json`. Endpoints: `/info`, `/pair`, projects, spaces, sets, one set, sessions, session, waiting, screen. No events yet; a reply carries `epoch` and `revision` from the counter, which only the diff of A3 will move. The screen is answered on the frame as the control port answers it (a pane snapshot, redacted); the worker handoff arrives with the screen cache of A4, since there is nothing to version before it. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status.* Tests: `tests/remote.rs` against a real socket with fakes, modelled on `tests/control.rs`, covering pairing, the pin check, scope, revocation, the allowlist and screen redaction; a UI test for the dialog. Acceptance: a paired `curl` with the pinned certificate reads every view over the LAN; an unpaired one gets `/info` and nothing else.
441:**A4 — Watched content.** The watch set and its worker poll, `watch` and `unwatch` with `watching`, content versions for screen (the other content kinds arrive with Milestone C and use the same cache), eviction, the policy fingerprint in the cache key, the overflow close. *Built 2026-10-12; see design.md's remote client status. The worker reads a pane's whole window so a short read and the poll see one version; the policy is resolved and cached on the frame (cleared by any save or secret change) until Milestone C moves the secret reads off it; a key held only by a subscriber has no read time and goes with its last `unwatch`.* Acceptance: a watched pane's screen updates live while the host shows an unrelated view or is hidden; the abuse tests of §4.1 pass against the real adapter.

200:  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
201:  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
202:  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".
203:
204:New read models, added to the wire crate:
205:
206:- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
207:- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
208:- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
209:- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
210:  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
211:  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
212:  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
213:  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
214:  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
215:  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
296:The ticket view on a device (2026-10-17) reads Dispatch through the Switchboard port, not Dispatch's own socket, which only the Mac reaches: the port serves what the app already holds from its two-second status poll, so a device costs the runner nothing. `GET dispatch/tickets` is the core's `TicketListing` (`src/core/tickets.rs`): `connected` (a runner answered the last poll; without one the tickets are the last seen), the `projects` with a pipeline (slots, running, pending, waiting on me, the queue, the supervisor's session id), and the `tickets` by project then oldest first, never the runner's write order. Each ticket is a summary: source, state and reason, the current stage's name among the `stages`, `standing` worded exactly as the Mac's page words it (`1 waiting on you`, `plan running`, `parked: <reason>`, `held: <why>`), `waits` and `urgent` as the page colours it, `current_session` and `root_project`, and every decision with its question, options, recommendation, `multiple`, state, answer and `needs_note`. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}` adds the body (bounded at the notes cap), the attempts with the session each ran in and the pull request it is bound to, the lanes by branch, and the holds; paths stay on the Mac. The collection is one resource, `tickets` with an empty id, fingerprinted with everything else: a decision made or answered, a stage moved, or the runner coming or going is one `changed` frame, to every subscriber.
297:
298:Two commands under `control`, each the Mac's own action and so Dispatch's own call: `decide` takes `{decision, answer, note?}` (the decision's id; for a `multiple` decision the options joined by commas) and is checked against the last status before anything runs (the decision pending, every option among the decision's, a note where the option needs one), and `resume` a parked ticket. The reply is deferred until Dispatch answers the call, through the same channel the content worker answers on: `{decision}` or `{ticket}` on success, the runner's reason as `failed` or `not_found`, `dispatch_off` (503) when no runner answers. A decision already answered as asked is answered again from the record, so a device that lost the reply repeats at no cost; one answered otherwise is `answered` (409). `info` lists `tickets` among the capabilities, and a client treats a host without it as having no tickets.
299:
300:The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.

302:## 5. Security and pairing
303:
304:A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
305:
306:- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
307:- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
308:- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
309:- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
310:- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
311:- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
312:- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
313:- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
314:- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
315:- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
316:- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.

lines: - **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
- at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
-  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;

+  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener, `/info` sixty and the page's three files (§4.3) a hundred and twenty (a reload is three requests); past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
- a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
- one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);

- the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;

**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:

- **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.

lines: New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).

-- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.

The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it, and no wire view carries it yet: the excerpt is not yet on the wire; it will be a redacted field of the session view, masked as the redaction list above says, moving with `changed {session}`.

- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.

- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
- the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);

lines: A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
+- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info`, `/pair` and the page's three static files (§4.3).

- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.

- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.

- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.

- **The web page (2026-10-22).** The remote port serves a browser page
  (`web/index.html`, `app.css`, `app.js`, embedded by `src/web.rs`) at
  `GET /`, `/app.css` and `/app.js`, before pairing, under a strict
  CSP. The pairing QR and "Copy invite" now carry one URL,
  `https://<ip>:<port>/#code=…&key=…&id=…` (`core::remote::pairing_invite`),
  so a phone's camera opens the page; the code rides in the fragment,
  which no request log can hold, and the page clears it before any
  request. The page pairs with `transport: "cookie"`, and the host sets
  the token as `switchboard_token_<server_id>` (`Secure; HttpOnly;
  SameSite=Strict; Path=/api/v1/`), which `authenticate` reads when no
  bearer is sent and which a revoked token's 401 clears. The page lists
  sessions by project with the waiting ones first, shows a Claude Code
  session's last response or any other session's screen, and sends a
  reply under `control` scope; it polls over `fetch` and upgrades to
  the WebSocket when the browser allows one. The browser's trust step
  is the certificate warning (see `docs/remote-client.md` §5); the
  native clients still parse the earlier JSON invite. Not verified on
  a phone from here: whether a browser stores the `Secure` cookie from
  a bypassed-certificate origin, and whether iOS Safari carries the
  bypass to `wss://`.
- **Known gaps at the first merge.**

# Changelog

Every user-visible change goes under Unreleased as it lands.
`scripts/bump.sh` moves that section under the next version with the
date, and `scripts/release.sh` publishes that section as the release
notes. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com)
and the versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.4.1] - 2026-10-21

- Dispatch takes an issue once per project rather than once across the data directory, so a second project on the same repository can take an issue the first already holds.

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-21

### Added

- Dispatch reports each ticket's tokens by model and agent time, per attempt, stage and ticket, in `dispatch report` and a Usage tab on the ticket page.

### Fixed

- The session page's token count counts each message once, not once per content block, skips Claude Code's synthetic messages, and names each model when a session used more than one.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-19

### Added

- A session can be opened from the headset: a plus button on the Sessions tab, or "New session in this project" on a listed session, opens a Claude Code, Codex or shell session in a project on any connected host paired under the control scope, in the project's root or a directory under it, with a first message for an agent; the new session's window opens on the reply. The remote port takes `POST projects/{id}/sessions` for it and lists `create` among its capabilities.
- The remote port serves Dispatch's tickets: a listing with each ticket's standing and decisions, one ticket with its body, attempts and lanes, and under the control scope a decision answered or a parked ticket resumed. The headset gets a Tickets tab on it.
- The headset reads what each stage produced: every attempt lists its notes and other artifacts, its checks log, its review rounds' findings and responses and its evidence, each opened with a tap as text or as a picture; a ticket's timeline is read from the runner's event log; and a closable ticket can be closed. The ticket list is ordered last moved first, with a menu for the order (waiting first, newest, by project), the hosts, projects and states (closed hidden unless asked) and a "waiting on me" switch.

### Changed

- The headset's conversation view follows the end as a mode: it is held at the end, nothing growing under it can leave it behind, and a button at the right edge releases it for reading; the ellipsis at the foot returns it to following. Before, a new turn that began with a tool call could push the end off screen and switch following off, and the view could jump up to the turn it last held at the top.

### Fixed

- The headset's filter menu no longer jumps back to its top every couple of seconds while open: it is rebuilt only when a host or a session state it lists changes, not on every refresh.

## [0.2.1] - 2026-10-15

### Fixed

- A first launch on a display macOS reports at an odd scale (a Sidecar
  screen) no longer aborts before the window shows: the GPU's own
  texture limit is asked for instead of egui's 8192 (#185).

## [0.2.0] - 2026-10-15

### Added

- The app's version in the Settings menu, with a check for a newer
  release on GitHub twenty seconds after launch and hourly after that.
  A newer one is offered for download, checked against its published
  checksum and the running app's signing team, and installed on
  "Restart to update", which quits, swaps the bundle in place and
  relaunches.
- The headset pairs with a discovered host by its typed code, with the
  host's key shown for a check by eye, since visionOS gives an app no
  camera.
- `scripts/bump.sh` and `scripts/release.sh`: the version, this
  changelog and a GitHub release with the signed bundle and its
  checksum.
- The host's `/info` reply names the app's version, and the headset
  shows it beside each known host.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-10-14

### Added

- The remote port and the visionOS client: pairing with a pinned key,
  sessions and working sets from several hosts, live screens,
  conversations, run output, the draft and dictation into the host's
  editor, commands under the control scope.
- The first GitHub release, built by hand.

# Implementation notes for #230 (web control surface on the remote port)

## Commit
- `abe87c6` "Remote port serves a browser page paired from the invite URL" (one commit, as the plan names; contract additions are in its message). Not pushed, no PR.
- Before the commit: `cargo fmt --all`, `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --locked --workspace` (all green; tests/remote.rs 49, tests/ui.rs 205), the dispatch Linux-target clippy, and `swift test --package-path client --filter FixturesTests` (green, includes `testInviteParsesTheURL`). Tree clean after the commit.

## What was built
- Adapter (`src/adapters/remote.rs`): `RemoteRequest::cookies` (only `switchboard_token_*` pairs kept), `RemoteReply::headers`, `respond` takes the reply (Content-Type defaults to JSON unless a header gives one), `PAGE_PER_MINUTE = 120` window for `/`, `/app.css`, `/app.js`.
- Frame (`src/app.rs`): exact-match static replies with CSP, `no-store`, `nosniff` (via `remote_off_api`/`page_reply`); `authenticate` takes bearer first, then this host's cookie, and clears the cookie (`Max-Age=0`) on a 401 from the host's own cookie only; `remote_pair` honours `transport: "cookie"`.
- Core: `pairing_invite`, `token_cookie_name`; `core::remote` is now `pub mod` so tests and the UI can reach them (the plan did not say this; the module was private).
- Page: `web/index.html`, `web/app.css`, `web/app.js`, embedded by `src/web.rs`. Poll by default; the WebSocket opens after the first `/waiting` reply and the poll covers a dropped socket.
- UI: QR and Copy invite carry the URL; the dialog sentence reworded; no QR or Copy invite without a network address.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` takes the URL form; new `client/Fixtures/invite.txt` and `testInviteParsesTheURL`.
- Docs: remote-client.md (§4.1, §4.3, §5, §13 row, the excerpt sentence), design.md status bullet and known gaps, README (Layout rows, dev-aid paragraph), client README, CHANGELOG.

## Fallbacks and unresolved facts (built as the plan says, not settled)
- Cookie on a bypassed-certificate origin: built the cookie transport only; the page shows "pair again" when its first authenticated call is refused. The `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` transport is not built. **Not tested on a phone**; the plan's "test this first on a phone" step could not be done here (no device), so Decision 2 is unverified.
- iOS Safari `wss://` after a bypass: poll is the default, socket is the enhancement.
- Safari bypass persistence, `replaceState` and history, browser retry of a dropped page-load connection: nothing added beyond what the plan states.
- The acceptance steps from the issue (one phone) were not run.

## Where the plan was wrong or loose
- Plan said `core::remote::...` functions; the module was private (`mod remote;`) and had to become `pub mod remote;`.
- Plan said the `http` test helper gains a `cookie` argument. I kept `http` unchanged for its call sites and added `http_with` (bearer and cookie, returns headers) and `call_raw`; `subscribe_at` delegates to a new `subscribe_with`, with a `subscribe_cookie` wrapper.
- README Layout line numbers in the plan (383, 401, 423, 437, 446) did not match; I found the rows by content. The `client/` row did not need a change.
- `a_page_load_fits_the_stranger_pool`: the 4th connection (`/waiting` with the cookie) closes after its reply, so the slot would free either way; the test still proves the sequence (three held page connections, authenticated call, socket upgrade) fits.
- The UI test would fail on a host with no network address (Copy invite is now absent then); it checks `local_address()` and asserts the absence in that case.
- `invite.txt` was written by hand from the existing fixture identity (`info.json`/`pin.json`) rather than regenerating every fixture with `SWITCHBOARD_WRITE_FIXTURES=1`, which would have churned all fixtures with a new key. The Rust fixture test asserts the file equals `pairing_invite(..)` over that identity.
- The UI previously formatted an IPv6 address without brackets (`{ip}:{port}`); it now uses `SocketAddr` so it is bracketed.
- No schema bump: no serialized type changed (SCHEMA_VERSION untouched).
- Scripted edits (python/perl/heredocs) were blocked in this session, so edits were made by hand.

content.text:
I built the plan as a single commit, `abe87c6` ("Remote port serves a browser page paired from the invite URL"), with the plan's contract additions listed in its message. I didn't push or open a pull request, and `git status` is empty.

fmt, clippy (workspace, and the dispatch Linux-target check) and the full workspace tests all pass, and so do the Swift fixture tests, including the new URL-parsing one. I never ran the page in a real browser, so everything about how it behaves on a phone is untested. In particular I did not do the plan's first step: testing on a phone whether the cookie survives the certificate bypass. I built only the cookie transport; the page shows "pair again" if the first authenticated call after pairing is refused. The `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` fallback is not built. The page polls by default, with the WebSocket as the upgrade, which covers the iOS Safari `wss://` question. The issue's one-phone acceptance steps were not run.

Where the plan was off, or I diverged from it:
- **`core::remote` was private.** It is now `pub mod remote`, so tests and the UI can reach `pairing_invite` and `token_cookie_name`.
- **Test helper.** I left `http` unchanged and added `http_with` and `call_raw` for the cookie and header cases, instead of changing every call site.
- **Invite fixture.** I wrote `client/Fixtures/invite.txt` by hand from the existing fixture identity, so no other fixture changed. A Rust test checks it equals `pairing_invite(..)`.
- **README line numbers.** The plan's were stale, so I found the Layout rows by content.
- **Pool test.** In `a_page_load_fits_the_stranger_pool` the fourth connection closes after its reply, so its slot frees anyway. The test still covers the sequence: three held page connections, an authenticated call, then the socket upgrade.
- **No network address.** The dialog now shows no QR and no Copy invite then, so the UI test checks for that case.
- **IPv6 in the dialog.** It was shown without brackets before; it is now bracketed.

There is no `SCHEMA_VERSION` bump, since no serialized type changed. My notes are in `notes.md` under the stage directory.
